newsitem.title: SWAZILAND: Unions end goods block from entering Swaziland.
newsitem.headline: Unions end goods block from entering Swaziland.

text.p: Unions blocked the borders of the tiny landlocked kingdom of Swaziland on Monday ahead of talks with the Swazi government to press for democratic change, union leaders said.

Heavily armed soldiers and police patrolled both sides of the border where members of the Swaziland Federation of Trade Unions (SFTU) and the mighty Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) prevented goods trucks from travelling through.

"We think the blockade has been very successful because a lot of trucks have not even bothered to try and come through here...and those that have, have been stopped," SFTU official Jabu Nxumalo told Reuters.
"We hope that this drastic action will knock some sense into the heads of government before we start negotiations on Wednesday," he added.
The federation began a nationwide strike four weeks ago to demand the repeal of a 1973 royal decree that vested all state powers in the monarchy and banned political parties.
It was patchily observed and the blockade was called to put extra pressure on Swaziland's monarchy.
Nxumalo said the union had suspended the strike and workers would return to work on Wednesday.
He added, however, that the union would call for a two-day strike the first week of every month to maintain pressure.

Swaziland's two major foreign exchange earners, the sugar and timber industries, have been hardest hit by the strike with a 100-percent stayaway in these two belts. The sugar industry has said it stands to lose up to $700,000 a day.
A lack of unity among the unions meant, however, that other factories had largely escaped the call for a nationwide strike over the last month.
Cosatu deputy secretary general Zwelinzima Vavi said the South African unions would continue to support the SFTU.
"We will take more action if these negotiations fail...We will muster a three-day blockade which will be much more effective," he told Reuters.
Swaziland, with a population of 900,000, is heavily dependent on South Africa, which absorbs over half its exports.
By late afternoon the blockade ended without incident.
"They've all gone home now. It has been very peaceful," police spokesman Captain Eben Grove said.
After a violent strike last year, King Mswati III set up a review commission to make recommendations on drawing up a constitutional democracy.
The commission, which has two years in which to make its findings, has irked the union federation which says it is not representative and listens only to submissions made by individuals.
